title: Drowning in Data
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien argues that schools are very good at collecting data and poor at using it, so that data piles up as a hoarding problem rather than driving change. He sets out the human biases that distort analysis, namely the instinct to look for negatives and then build a narrative that excuses them, and the way predicted-versus-achieved measures can flatter or mislead. His response is a faculty-meeting protocol that makes staff record neutral observations about the numbers (a fact, something interesting, a trend) before any explanation is attempted. He also models sharing his own worst data so colleagues feel safe doing the same, and keeps negative findings at whole-team level. He critiques student surveys, warning against confusing student voice with student agency and recommending questions tied to explicit teaching priorities. He closes by separating performance in checks for understanding from learning, which needs spaced retrieval, and insists on quality over quantity of data.
points: Staff need to feel safe sharing their own data before any improvement conversation can happen, and Brien models this by showing his worst results first.
A three-step objective protocol (note a fact, something interesting, a trend) delays the explanatory story that people use to protect their own practice.
Student survey data should not steer lesson planning; questions should be aligned to school priorities and explained to students, such as whether the teacher breaks information into small chunks.
Checks for understanding show whether instruction worked, not whether learning has occurred, which requires spaced retrieval over weeks and months.
Data collected to confirm a pre-chosen solution is worthless; the test is whether it informs meaningful change.
quotes: Everything is data and data is everywhere. Just you clicking on this post adds a digit to the view count on this post and compares the current views with average views. Your smart watch collects and analyses your heart rate data and stress day in and day out. Your phone tracks and reports on your screen time. We have so much data, but data is only as useful if it is interpreted and actioned effectively.

We are incredible at collecting data, but are we starting to form a hoarding problem? How much of that data informs meaningful change? Even worse, how much data is collected solely as evidence to ‘achieve’ a short term goal that will never be spoken about again as priorities shift to the next shiny new teaching fad

One of the biggest flaws with the way we naturally tend to analyze data as human beings and professionals is that we do two things instantly; first we look for the negatives, then we build a narrator that explains those negatives so we do not have to question the quality of our teaching practice. This takes what should be an objective measure and makes it entirely subjective.

This has meant that when it comes to analyzing data we’ve tried to put protocols in place which force staff members to look at the data from a curious, fact driven perspective first and then use those facts to conduct our detective work to create an action plan for improvement.
Letting student survey data decide how we plan lessons would be like letting patient survey data decide how a surgeon conducts an operation.

Checks for understanding alone are a poor proxy for learning. They look and sound incredible. They can help to create a positive feedback look where students are able to have misconceptions corrected and genuine intrinsic motivation. However without consistent spaced retrieval, checks for understanding are a poor proxy for learning as without rehearsal and review over the coming weeks and months, students will be fighting a losing battle against forgetting.

Too often do we find (or create) a problem then deliberately collect biased data that says we solved that problem despite no meaningful change occurring. It is the equivalent of making the test so easy that all students get 100% and if we reported that data home to parents, I do not think it would hold up to scrutiny.
